citation: Finkelstein, N., Hanson, T., Huang, C.-W., Hirschman, B., & Huang, M. (2010). Effects of Problem Based Economics on high school economics instruction (NCEE 2010-4002). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education.
report_number: NCEE 2010-4002 (REL West; prepared by WestEd under contract ED-06C0-0014)
design: Cluster-randomized controlled trial; unit of assignment = teacher (class-level); 128 economics teachers from 106 high schools in Arizona and California randomized 1:1 (64 intervention / 64 control); after post-randomization teacher attrition the final student analytic sample = 4,350 students from 64 teachers (2,502 students/35 teachers intervention; 1,848 students/29 teachers control); subject = economics (STEM-adjacent social science); grades 11-12 (88% grade 12, 12% grade 11). Intervention = Problem Based Economics curriculum (Buck Institute) plus teacher professional development and support; counterfactual = business-as-usual high school economics with teachers' regular annual PD. Impact estimates from conditional multilevel (HLM) regression models with students nested in teachers, adjusting for baseline covariates.
problems: Single TPD arm vs single business-as-usual control (registry row 30). Two co-primary student achievement outcomes reported (TEL content knowledge; performance-task problem-solving) -- both extracted as outcome_role=primary; they are distinct constructs, not a composite/subscale pair. The report gives effect sizes as impact/control-group-SD and the impact estimates + SEs come from the multilevel (HLM) model, so g is essentially d with a negligible J small-sample correction and clustering is already accounted for (cluster_adjusted=true). ICC values recorded are the study's estimated/unconditional intraclass correlations from the final analytic samples (Table A.1, p. 61: 0.24 for TEL, 0.12 for performance task); the 0.15/0.20 ICCs mentioned elsewhere were planning-stage assumptions and were NOT used. Per-arm Ns are the outcome response counts from Table 2.5 (TEL: 2,178 int / 1,574 ctrl = 3,752; performance task: 1,918 int / 1,497 ctrl = 3,415) which match the analytic sample sizes in Table 4.1. No raw posttest SDs by group beyond the adjusted-mean SDs shown in Table 4.1 are given; standardizing SD is the control-group SD per the report's note. Note: the IES PDF filename is REL_20104012 but the official report number on the title/citation page is NCEE 2010-4002.

effect_sizes.arm_label: Problem Based Economics (curriculum + teacher PD) vs business-as-usual economics
effect_sizes.test_name: Test of Economic Literacy (TEL), 40-item standardized economics achievement test (Walstad & Rebeck 2001)
effect_sizes.timepoint: post (end of spring 2008 semester, end of one-semester economics course)
effect_sizes.g_method: Reported effect size = impact / control-group SD = 2.60 / 8.21 = 0.31669 (paper reports 0.32, Table 4.1, Model C). Hedges' g = J*d with J = 1 - 3/(4*df-1), df = n_t+n_c-2 = 3750, J = 0.99980; g = 0.99980 * 0.31669 = 0.31662. g_se = J * (impact_se / control SD) = 0.99980 * (1.09/8.21) = 0.13274; g_var = g_se^2 = 0.017619. Standardized by the control-group SD (8.21) of the TEL posttest, per the report's effect-size note.
effect_sizes.page_ref: Table 4.1 (p. 53); Exec. Summary (p. xi); per-arm n from Table 2.5 (p. 34); ICC from Table A.1 (p. 61)
effect_sizes.notes: Primary confirmatory outcome #1 (student content knowledge). Adjusted means: intervention 22.61, control 20.01; difference 2.60 (SE 1.09), significant p=0.017 (BH-adjusted p=0.034). Effect size 0.32 favoring TPD. Impact from conditional HLM (students nested in teachers) adjusting for baseline covariates incl. student TEL pretest where available (Model C is the headline model; sensitivity Models A/B and alternative samples give ES 0.17-0.34, Appendix Table I.1). cluster_adjusted=true because impact estimate and SE come from the multilevel model that accounts for teacher-level clustering. n_t=2178/n_c=1574 are TEL response counts (Table 2.5) = 3,752 analytic N (Table 4.1). icc=0.24 is the estimated intraclass correlation from the final analytic sample (Table A.1). SDs shown (8.08/8.21) accompany the adjusted means in Table 4.1; control SD 8.21 is the standardizing SD.

effect_sizes.arm_label: Problem Based Economics (curriculum + teacher PD) vs business-as-usual economics
effect_sizes.test_name: Performance task assessment composite score (5 open-ended economics problem-solving tasks developed by UCLA CRESST; each student randomly assigned 2 tasks; composite range 4-12)
effect_sizes.timepoint: post (end of spring 2008 semester, end of one-semester economics course)
effect_sizes.g_method: Reported effect size = impact / control-group SD = 0.54 / 2.01 = 0.26866 (paper reports 0.27, Table 4.1, Model C). Hedges' g = J*d with J = 1 - 3/(4*df-1), df = n_t+n_c-2 = 3413, J = 0.99978; g = 0.99978 * 0.26866 = 0.26860. g_se = J * (impact_se / control SD) = 0.99978 * (0.24/2.01) = 0.11938; g_var = g_se^2 = 0.014251. Standardized by the control-group SD (2.01) of the performance-task composite, per the report's effect-size note.
effect_sizes.page_ref: Table 4.1 (p. 53); Exec. Summary (p. xi); per-arm n from Table 2.3/2.5 (pp. 28, 34); ICC from Table A.1 (p. 61)
effect_sizes.notes: Primary confirmatory outcome #2 (student problem-solving skills). Adjusted means: intervention 6.72, control 6.18; difference 0.54 (SE 0.24), significant p=0.024 (BH-adjusted p=0.024). Effect size 0.27 favoring TPD. Researcher/developer-made open-ended performance assessment (UCLA CRESST), not a standardized norm-referenced test, so test_type=researcher_made (would likely be filtered centrally as the meta-analysis used independent measures; extracted and labeled per spec). Impact from conditional HLM model (Model C headline; sensitivity Models A/B give ES 0.09-0.27, Appendix Table I.2). cluster_adjusted=true (multilevel model SE). n_t=1918/n_c=1497 from Table 2.3/2.5 = 3,415 analytic N (Table 4.1). n_clusters=62 and icc=0.12 are from Table A.1 for the performance-task analytic sample (fewer than the 64 teachers in the TEL analysis because some teachers had no students with valid performance-task scores).
